items.stem: Which term is defined as "a white blood cell that engulfs and digests pathogens and debris by phagocytosis, such as a neutrophil or macrophage"?
items.answer: Phagocyte
items.markingKey: Phagocyte: a white blood cell that engulfs and digests pathogens and debris by phagocytosis, such as a neutrophil or macrophage.

items.stem: Describe and explain how a neutrophil destroys a bacterium.
items.answer: Attracted by chemicals (chemotaxis); receptors bind bacterium; engulfs by endocytosis into a phagocytic vesicle; lysosomes fuse and release hydrolytic enzymes; bacterium digested.
items.markingKey: any 4 from: Attracted by chemicals (chemotaxis); receptors bind bacterium; engulfs by endocytosis into a phagocytic vesicle; lysosomes fuse and release hydrolytic enzymes; bacterium digested (1 mark each) [4]

items.stem: Explain the role of macrophages in linking the non-specific and specific immune responses.
items.answer: Macrophages engulf pathogens, partly digest them and display antigens on their surface (antigen-presenting cells); these activate specific T helper lymphocytes.
items.markingKey: Macrophages engulf pathogens [1]; partly digest them and display antigens on their surface (antigen-presenting cells) [1]; these activate specific T helper lymphocytes [1] [3]

items.stem: Felix examined a stained blood smear and counted 250 white blood cells: neutrophils 175, lymphocytes 62, monocytes 10, others 3. (a) Calculate the percentage of each of neutrophils and lymphocytes. (b) The total white cell count is 7 × 10⁹ dm⁻³. Calculate the number of neutrophils per dm³.
items.answer: (a) neutrophils 70%; lymphocytes 24.8% (b) 4.9 × 10⁹ dm⁻³

items.stem: Ravi examined a stained blood smear and counted 100 white blood cells: neutrophils 58, lymphocytes 24, monocytes 7, others 11. (a) Calculate the percentage of each of neutrophils and lymphocytes. (b) The total white cell count is 6.5 × 10⁹ dm⁻³. Calculate the number of neutrophils per dm³. (c) Describe how you would distinguish a neutrophil from a lymphocyte in the smear.
items.answer: (a) neutrophils 58%; lymphocytes 24% (b) 3.77 × 10⁹ dm⁻³ (c) Neutrophil: lobed nucleus, granular cytoplasm, larger (10–12 μm). Lymphocyte: large round nucleus filling most of the cell, little cytoplasm, smaller (about 7 μm).
items.markingKey: (a) 58 ÷ 100 × 100 = 58% [1]; 24 ÷ 100 × 100 = 24% [1] (b) 0.58 × 6.5 × 10⁹ = 3.77 × 10⁹ [2] (c) neutrophil lobed nucleus [1]; lymphocyte large round nucleus / little cytoplasm [1] [6]

items.stem: A pathology lecturer in Colombo describes the body's response to Staphylococcus bacteria entering a cut on the hand. (a) Explain how phagocytes reach the site of infection. (b) State one difference between the role of neutrophils and macrophages.
items.answer: (a) Damaged cells and pathogens release chemicals (e.g. histamine) causing inflammation; capillaries become leaky; phagocytes squeeze out and move towards chemicals (chemotaxis). (b) Macrophages present antigens to lymphocytes / are long-lived; neutrophils are short-lived first responders.
items.markingKey: (a) Damaged cells and pathogens release chemicals (e.g. histamine) causing inflammation [1]; capillaries become leaky [1]; phagocytes squeeze out and move towards chemicals (chemotaxis) [1] [3] (b) Macrophages present antigens to lymphocytes / are long-lived; neutrophils are short-lived first responders [1]

items.stem: Explain why there are many lysosomes in phagocytes.
items.answer: Many pathogens are engulfed; lysosomes supply hydrolytic enzymes to digest them.
items.markingKey: Many pathogens are engulfed [1]; lysosomes supply hydrolytic enzymes to digest them [1] [2]

items.stem: A student in Mexico City states: "Phagocytes only attack one type of pathogen." Explain why this statement is incorrect.
items.answer: Phagocytes are non-specific and engulf many types.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: identifies the error / statement is incorrect; 1 mark: Phagocytes are non-specific and engulf many types. [2]

items.stem: Give a reason for each answer. (a) Explain why there are many lysosomes in phagocytes. (b) Explain the role of macrophages in linking the non-specific and specific immune responses.
items.answer: (a) Many pathogens are engulfed; lysosomes supply hydrolytic enzymes to digest them. (b) Macrophages engulf pathogens, partly digest them and display antigens on their surface (antigen-presenting cells); these activate specific T helper lymphocytes.
items.markingKey: (a) Many pathogens are engulfed [1]; lysosomes supply hydrolytic enzymes to digest them [1] [2] (b) Macrophages engulf pathogens [1]; partly digest them and display antigens on their surface (antigen-presenting cells) [1]; these activate specific T helper lymphocytes [1] [3]

items.stem: Yusuf examined a stained blood smear and counted 250 white blood cells: neutrophils 149, lymphocytes 56, monocytes 17, others 28. (a) Calculate the percentage of each of neutrophils and lymphocytes. (b) The total white cell count is 8 × 10⁹ dm⁻³. Calculate the number of neutrophils per dm³.
items.answer: (a) neutrophils 59.6%; lymphocytes 22.4% (b) 4.77 × 10⁹ dm⁻³

items.stem: Describe the origin and roles of neutrophils and macrophages and explain how phagocytosis destroys pathogens.
items.answer: Both from bone marrow stem cells; neutrophils short-lived, lobed nucleus, first responders; monocytes → macrophages in tissues, long-lived, antigen presentation. Phagocytosis: chemotaxis, binding, endocytosis, phagosome, lysosomes, hydrolytic enzymes, digestion.
items.markingKey: origin [1]; neutrophils [1]; macrophages / antigen presentation [2]; phagocytosis steps [3] [7]

items.stem: A pathology lecturer in Singapore describes the body's response to Staphylococcus bacteria entering a cut on the hand. (a) Describe phagocytosis by a neutrophil. (b) Explain how antibodies make phagocytosis more effective.
items.answer: (a) Chemicals released by pathogens and damaged cells attract phagocytes (chemotaxis) → Receptors on the phagocyte bind to the pathogen → The cell surface membrane extends around the pathogen and engulfs it by endocytosis → A phagocytic vesicle (phagosome) forms → Lysosomes fuse with the vesicle and release hydrolytic enzymes → The pathogen is digested and the products are absorbed or removed. (b) Antibodies act as opsonins / cause agglutination; phagocytes have receptors for antibodies, so they bind and engulf pathogens more easily.
items.markingKey: (a) any 4 from: Chemicals released by pathogens and damaged cells attract phagocytes (chemotaxis); Receptors on the phagocyte bind to the pathogen; The cell surface membrane extends around the pathogen and engulfs it by endocytosis; A phagocytic vesicle (phagosome) forms; Lysosomes fuse with the vesicle and release hydrolytic enzymes; The pathogen is digested and the products are absorbed or removed (1 mark each) [4] (b) Antibodies act as opsonins / cause agglutination [1]; phagocytes have receptors for antibodies, so they bind and engulf pathogens more easily [1] [2]

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "a lymphocyte that matures in the bone marrow and, when activated, divides to form plasma cells that secrete antibodies and memory cells"?
items.answer: B lymphocyte
items.markingKey: B lymphocyte: a lymphocyte that matures in the bone marrow and, when activated, divides to form plasma cells that secrete antibodies and memory cells.

items.stem: Explain how clonal selection leads to the production of antibodies against a specific antigen.
items.answer: Each B cell has receptors for one antigen; the B cell with complementary receptors binds the antigen; stimulated by T helper cytokines, it divides by mitosis (clonal expansion); differentiates into plasma cells secreting the specific antibody and memory cells.
items.markingKey: Each B cell has receptors for one antigen [1]; the B cell with complementary receptors binds the antigen [1]; stimulated by T helper cytokines, it divides by mitosis (clonal expansion) [1]; differentiates into plasma cells secreting the specific antibody and memory cells [1] [4]

items.stem: Explain why the immune system does not usually attack the body's own cells.
items.answer: During development, lymphocytes with receptors complementary to self antigens are destroyed, so only those recognising non-self antigens remain.
items.markingKey: any 2 from: During development; lymphocytes with receptors complementary to self antigens are destroyed; so only those recognising non-self antigens remain (1 mark each) [2]

items.stem: A volunteer in Mumbai was injected with an antigen on day 0 and again on day 35. After the first injection, antibody was first detected after 7 days and peaked at 15 arbitrary units. After the second injection, antibody was detected after 2 days and peaked at 225 arbitrary units. Suggest why the antibody concentration falls after each peak.
items.answer: Antigen has been removed so plasma cells stop secreting / die; antibodies are broken down.
items.markingKey: Antigen has been removed so plasma cells stop secreting / die [1]; antibodies are broken down [1] [2]

items.stem: A volunteer in Cairo was injected with an antigen on day 0 and again on day 35. After the first injection, antibody was first detected after 10 days and peaked at 25 arbitrary units. After the second injection, antibody was detected after 3 days and peaked at 200 arbitrary units. (a) Explain why there is a delay before antibodies appear after the first injection. (b) Suggest why the antibody concentration falls after each peak.
items.answer: (a) Few lymphocytes have complementary receptors; time needed for clonal selection, activation by T helper cells, division and differentiation into plasma cells. (b) Antigen has been removed so plasma cells stop secreting / die; antibodies are broken down.
items.markingKey: (a) Few lymphocytes have complementary receptors [1]; time needed for clonal selection, activation by T helper cells, division and differentiation into plasma cells [1] [2] (b) Antigen has been removed so plasma cells stop secreting / die [1]; antibodies are broken down [1] [2]

items.stem: A volunteer in Seoul was injected with an antigen on day 0 and again on day 35. After the first injection, antibody was first detected after 10 days and peaked at 10 arbitrary units. After the second injection, antibody was detected after 4 days and peaked at 150 arbitrary units. (a) Calculate how many times greater the peak concentration was after the second injection. (b) Explain the differences between the primary and secondary responses.
items.answer: (a) 15 (b) Memory cells produced in the primary response are present in larger numbers; they recognise the antigen quickly, divide rapidly and form many plasma cells, so antibody is made sooner and in greater amounts.
items.markingKey: (a) 150 ÷ 10 = 15 [1] (b) memory cells [1]; faster clonal expansion [1]; more plasma cells / antibody [1] [3]

items.stem: A child in Lima is infected with influenza virus for the first time. (a) Explain how T killer cells help to end the infection. (b) Explain why the child is unlikely to suffer from the disease if infected again.
items.answer: (a) Recognise viral antigens on infected cells; bind and destroy them, so virus cannot replicate. (b) Memory cells give a fast, large secondary response, destroying the virus before symptoms develop (active immunity).
items.markingKey: (a) Recognise viral antigens on infected cells [1]; bind and destroy them, so virus cannot replicate [1] [2] (b) any 2 from: Memory cells give a fast; large secondary response; destroying the virus before symptoms develop (active immunity) (1 mark each) [2]

items.stem: A child in Hanoi is infected with hepatitis B virus for the first time. (a) Describe the roles of T helper cells in the response. (b) Explain why the child is unlikely to suffer from the disease if infected again.
items.answer: (a) Bind to antigens presented by macrophages; divide; release cytokines that stimulate B cells (to divide and secrete antibody) and T killer cells and macrophages. (b) Memory cells give a fast, large secondary response, destroying the virus before symptoms develop (active immunity).
items.markingKey: (a) Bind to antigens presented by macrophages [1]; divide [1]; release cytokines that stimulate B cells (to divide and secrete antibody) and T killer cells and macrophages [1] [3] (b) any 2 from: Memory cells give a fast; large secondary response; destroying the virus before symptoms develop (active immunity) (1 mark each) [2]

items.stem: Which is the correct definition of the term "T helper cell"?
options: An activated B lymphocyte that secretes large amounts of antibody.
A T lymphocyte that attaches to and destroys infected body cells displaying a specific antigen.
A T lymphocyte that releases cytokines to stimulate B cells to divide and secrete antibodies, and to activate T killer cells and macrophages.
A long-lived lymphocyte that remains after an immune response and responds quickly if the same antigen enters the body again.
items.answer: A T lymphocyte that releases cytokines to stimulate B cells to divide and secrete antibodies, and to activate T killer cells and macrophages.
items.markingKey: T helper cell: a T lymphocyte that releases cytokines to stimulate B cells to divide and secrete antibodies, and to activate T killer cells and macrophages.

items.stem: Where do T lymphocytes mature?
items.answer: In the thymus
items.markingKey: B cells mature in bone marrow; T cells in the thymus.

items.stem: Explain how T killer cells destroy virus-infected cells.
items.answer: Infected cells display viral antigens on their surface; T killer cells with complementary receptors bind and release chemicals (perforins) that make holes in the membrane, killing the cell.
items.markingKey: Infected cells display viral antigens on their surface [1]; T killer cells with complementary receptors bind and release chemicals (perforins) that make holes in the membrane [1]; killing the cell [1] [3]

items.stem: What is the name for "the part of an antibody that is the same in all antibodies of a class and binds to receptors on phagocytes"?
items.answer: Constant region
items.markingKey: Constant region: the part of an antibody that is the same in all antibodies of a class and binds to receptors on phagocytes.

items.stem: Explain how the structure of an antibody is related to its function.
items.answer: Variable regions form two specific antigen-binding sites complementary to one antigen; two sites allow agglutination; hinge gives flexibility; constant region binds phagocyte receptors; disulfide bonds stabilise the structure.
items.markingKey: any 4 from: Variable regions form two specific antigen-binding sites complementary to one antigen; two sites allow agglutination; hinge gives flexibility; constant region binds phagocyte receptors; disulfide bonds stabilise the structure (1 mark each) [4]

items.stem: Explain why each antibody binds to only one antigen.
items.answer: The amino acid sequence of the variable region determines a specific 3-D shape of the binding site, complementary only to that antigen.
items.markingKey: The amino acid sequence of the variable region determines a specific 3-D shape of the binding site [1]; complementary only to that antigen [1] [2]

items.stem: An IgG antibody contains two heavy chains of 446 amino acids and two light chains of 214 amino acids. (a) Calculate the total number of amino acids and the number of peptide bonds. (b) Name the bonds that hold the four chains together.
items.answer: (a) 1,320 amino acids; 1,316 peptide bonds (b) Disulfide bonds (with hydrogen bonds / other interactions)

items.stem: An IgG antibody contains two heavy chains of 446 amino acids and two light chains of 214 amino acids. (a) Calculate the total number of amino acids and the number of peptide bonds. (b) Name the bonds that hold the four chains together. (c) Explain why antibodies produced against different antigens have different amino acid sequences only in part of each chain.
items.answer: (a) 1,320 amino acids; 1,316 peptide bonds (b) Disulfide bonds (with hydrogen bonds / other interactions) (c) The variable regions differ to give binding sites complementary to different antigens; constant regions are the same so they bind the same phagocyte receptors.

items.stem: A patient in Hanoi is treated for exposure to snake venom with an injection of antibodies that bind to it. (a) Explain how the antibodies prevent snake venom harming the patient. (b) Explain why each antibody is specific to one antigen.
items.answer: (a) They bind to the toxin (neutralisation), changing / blocking its shape so it cannot bind to receptors on body cells; complexes are engulfed by phagocytes. (b) Variable region amino acid sequence gives a binding site complementary to one antigen.
items.markingKey: (a) They bind to the toxin (neutralisation), changing / blocking its shape so it cannot bind to receptors on body cells [1]; complexes are engulfed by phagocytes [1] [2] (b) Variable region amino acid sequence gives a binding site complementary to one antigen [2] [2]

items.stem: How many polypeptide chains make up a typical IgG antibody?
options: Three: one heavy and two light chains
Four: two heavy and two light chains
items.answer: Four: two heavy and two light chains
items.markingKey: Held together by disulfide bonds.

items.stem: Explain how agglutination helps the immune response.
items.answer: Each antibody binds two pathogens, clumping them; clumps cannot spread or enter cells and are easily engulfed by phagocytes.
items.markingKey: Each antibody binds two pathogens, clumping them [1]; clumps cannot spread or enter cells and are easily engulfed by phagocytes [1] [2]

items.stem: Elena says: "Antibodies kill bacteria by digesting them." Explain whether Elena is correct.
items.answer: Antibodies bind to antigens; phagocytes (or complement) destroy the pathogens.

items.stem: How many antigen-binding sites are there on 50 IgG antibody molecules?
items.markingKey: Each IgG has 2 binding sites: 50 × 2 = 100.

items.stem: Which term is defined as "immunity gained when an antigen stimulates the immune system to produce antibodies and memory cells"?
items.answer: Active immunity
items.markingKey: Active immunity: immunity gained when an antigen stimulates the immune system to produce antibodies and memory cells.

items.stem: Describe how monoclonal antibodies are produced.
items.answer: Inject a mouse with the antigen; extract B cells / plasma cells from spleen; fuse with myeloma cells to form hybridomas; select the hybridoma making the required antibody; culture it (cloned) to produce large amounts of identical antibody.
items.markingKey: any 4 from: Inject a mouse with the antigen; extract B cells / plasma cells from spleen; fuse with myeloma cells to form hybridomas; select the hybridoma making the required antibody; culture it (cloned) to produce large amounts of identical antibody (1 mark each) [4]

items.stem: Explain why vaccines often need booster injections.
items.answer: A second dose triggers a secondary response, producing more memory cells and a higher, longer-lasting antibody level.
items.markingKey: any 2 from: A second dose triggers a secondary response; producing more memory cells and a higher; longer-lasting antibody level (1 mark each) [2]

items.stem: For each example, state the type of immunity (natural or artificial, active or passive) and explain whether it is long-lasting: (i) a traveller given a yellow fever vaccine (ii) a child recovering from chickenpox.
items.answer: (i) Artificial active: the vaccine contains antigens that stimulate the person to make antibodies and memory cells; long-lasting (memory cells). (ii) Natural active: the child's own lymphocytes made antibodies and memory cells after infection; long-lasting (memory cells).
items.markingKey: (i) type [1]; duration with reason [1] (ii) type [1]; duration with reason [1] [4]

items.stem: For each example, state the type of immunity (natural or artificial, active or passive) and explain whether it is long-lasting: (i) a breastfed baby receiving antibodies in milk (ii) a traveller given a yellow fever vaccine.
items.answer: (i) Natural passive: antibodies are received from the mother; no memory cells are made; short-lived (no memory cells; antibodies broken down). (ii) Artificial active: the vaccine contains antigens that stimulate the person to make antibodies and memory cells; long-lasting (memory cells).
items.markingKey: (i) type [1]; duration with reason [1] (ii) type [1]; duration with reason [1] [4]

items.stem: A biotechnology company in Mumbai produces monoclonal antibodies for trastuzumab (Herceptin), which binds to HER2 receptors on breast cancer cells. (a) Explain how the antibodies are used in treatment. (b) Suggest one problem with using mouse antibodies to treat humans.
items.answer: (a) They bind to the receptors on cancer cells, blocking growth signals and marking the cells for destruction by the immune system. (b) They are recognised as foreign (non-self) antigens and trigger an immune response; so they are "humanised".

items.stem: Which type of immunity is shown by a child recovering from chickenpox?

items.stem: Explain how monoclonal antibodies can be used to diagnose a disease.
items.answer: They bind specifically to an antigen of the pathogen (or a marker molecule); linked to a dye / enzyme, they show whether the antigen is present (e.g. test strips).

items.stem: Give a reason for each answer. (a) Explain how the structure of an antibody is related to its function. (b) Explain how agglutination helps the immune response.
items.answer: (a) Variable regions form two specific antigen-binding sites complementary to one antigen; two sites allow agglutination; hinge gives flexibility; constant region binds phagocyte receptors; disulfide bonds stabilise the structure. (b) Each antibody binds two pathogens, clumping them; clumps cannot spread or enter cells and are easily engulfed by phagocytes.

items.stem: A pathology lecturer in Bangkok describes the body's response to Mycobacterium tuberculosis in the alveoli. (a) Explain how phagocytes reach the site of infection. (b) State one difference between the role of neutrophils and macrophages. (c) Suggest why pus forms at an infected cut.
